name: Sophie Germain
who: A French girl who taught herself mathematics from her father's books
story: Sophie Germain lived in Paris more than 200 years ago. As a teenager she read the books in her father's library and taught herself Latin and Greek so she could read even more. Her parents were not happy, but she kept learning. Later she wrote to famous mathematicians using a man's name, M. Le Blanc. The great mathematician Gauss praised her ideas about numbers, and later found out who she really was. Sophie loved prime numbers, which have exactly two factors: 1 and themselves. She studied primes p where 2 times p plus 1 is also prime. Today these are called Sophie Germain primes.
link: Today you hunt for factors, and Sophie studied prime numbers, the numbers with only two factors.
blurb: Sophie Germain taught herself maths from her father's books in Paris, over 200 years ago. She loved prime numbers, the numbers with exactly two factors.
q: Is 2 × 7 + 1 a prime? List the factors of your answer. Then try 5.
a: 2 x 7 + 1 = 15. The factors of 15 are 1, 3, 5 and 15, so 15 is not prime and 7 is not a Sophie Germain prime. For 5: 2 x 5 + 1 = 11, whose only factors are 1 and 11, so 11 is prime and 5 is a Sophie Germain prime.

name: Leonardo of Pisa (Fibonacci)
country: Italy (Pisa), schooled in Bugia, now Bejaia, Algeria
who: An Italian merchant's son who helped Europe learn the digits 0 to 9
story: Leonardo of Pisa, now called Fibonacci, lived about 800 years ago. His father was a merchant official who worked in Bugia, a trading town in North Africa that is now Bejaia in Algeria. As a boy Leonardo learned to count with ten digits, 0 to 9, where each digit's place gives its value. In 1202 he finished a book, the Liber Abaci, which showed merchants how to use these digits for money and trade. Place value is what lets ten digits write any big number, such as 47 305. Leonardo did not invent these digits, but his book helped them spread across Europe.
link: Today you read and build numbers up to 100 000, and place value is the idea that Leonardo's book helped spread.
blurb: Leonardo of Pisa (Fibonacci) learned the digits 0 to 9 as a boy in North Africa. His book, written in 1202, helped Europe use place value.
q: Use the digits 7, 0, 4, 9 and 2 once each. Write the biggest and the smallest 5-digit number you can.
a: Biggest: 97 420. Smallest: 20 479 (the 0 cannot go first, or it would not be a 5-digit number).

name: Katherine Johnson
who: A NASA mathematician who checked space-flight calculations
story: Katherine Johnson grew up in West Virginia in the USA. She was so quick at school that she was moved up several grades. She became a research mathematician at NASA, where in the early days people who did calculations were called computers. She worked out the flight path for Alan Shepard's 1961 flight, the first American in space. Before John Glenn orbited the Earth in 1962, accounts say he asked for Katherine to check the electronic computer's numbers by hand. Her answers matched. Checking an answer a second way is a habit every mathematician uses. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015.
link: Today you use add, subtract, multiply and divide, and Katherine's job was to get these calculations right and to check them.
blurb: Katherine Johnson was a NASA mathematician who worked out flight paths for early space flights. Accounts say astronauts trusted her to check calculations a second way.
q: Check that 6 × 48 = 288 using a different method from your first one. Hint: 48 is close to 50.
a: 6 x 50 = 300, and 6 x 2 = 12, so 6 x 48 = 300 - 12 = 288. It checks out. You can also check with division: 288 divided by 6 = 48.
label: Accounts say
legend_note: Accounts say John Glenn asked for her to check the numbers. The exact timing is uncertain and the film Hidden Figures dramatised the scene, so do not describe it as in the film.

name: Mahavira
who: An Indian maths teacher-writer who explained how to work with fractions
story: Mahavira lived in southern India about 1,200 years ago, around the year 850. We know almost nothing else about his life, not even exactly where he was born. We do know he wrote a maths book, the Ganita Sara Sangraha, while King Amoghavarsha ruled the land. One chapter explains how to work with fractions, including how to split a fraction into unit fractions, which have 1 on top. For example, the book shows that 2/17 can be written as 1/12 + 1/51 + 1/68. Splitting a fraction into smaller, friendlier pieces is a clever way to understand it.
link: Today you compare and change fractions, and Mahavira's book explained how to work with fractions and split them into unit fractions.
blurb: Mahavira, an Indian maths writer from about 1,200 years ago, wrote a book that explains how to work with fractions. It also shows how to split a fraction into unit fractions.
q: Show that 1/2 = 1/3 + 1/6 by making the denominators the same. Then split 3/4 into 1/2 plus a unit fraction.

name: Simon Stevin
who: A Flemish mathematician who wrote a short book to teach decimals to everyone
story: Simon Stevin was born in Bruges, in what is now Belgium, in 1548. He worked on many things, from the science of water to the science of weights. In 1585 he published a small book called The Tenth about decimal fractions. Stevin did not invent decimals, because others had used them before him. What he did was explain them clearly for the people who needed them. He said they would help surveyors, carpet-makers, wine-gaugers, mint-masters, stargazers and every kind of merchant. He showed how to split a whole into tenths, hundredths and thousandths. We still use decimals this way for money and measuring.
link: Today you work with tenths, hundredths and thousandths, which is exactly what Stevin's small book explained.
blurb: Simon Stevin, from Bruges, wrote a small book in 1585 that explained decimals clearly. He showed how to split a whole into tenths, hundredths and thousandths.
q: Write 3 + 4/10 + 5/100 as a decimal. Then add 2.8 to your answer.

name: Eratosthenes
country: Cyrene (now Libya) and Alexandria, Egypt; ancient Greek world
who: A Greek scholar who used a shadow angle to measure the Earth
story: Eratosthenes was a Greek scholar in the great library of Alexandria, Egypt, over 2,000 years ago. At noon on one day of the year, the Sun shone straight down a well in the town of Syene, so nothing had a shadow. On that day in Alexandria, an upright stick did make a shadow. He worked out that its angle was about 7.2 degrees, which is one fiftieth of a whole turn. So the two towns were one fiftieth of the way round the Earth. He multiplied the distance between them by 50. Historians are not sure how long his unit of distance was, so we cannot say how close he got.
link: Today you measure angles and turns, and Eratosthenes used the angle of a shadow to measure the whole Earth.
blurb: Eratosthenes, a Greek scholar in Egypt over 2,000 years ago, used the angle of a shadow to work out how big the Earth is. His angle was one fiftieth of a whole turn.
q: A whole turn is 360 degrees. If a shadow made an angle of 10 degrees, how many angles that size fit all the way round?
a: 360 divided by 10 = 36, so 36 angles. (Eratosthenes had about 7.2 degrees, and 360 divided by 7.2 = 50.)
legend_note: The exact length of a stadion is uncertain, so how close his answer was is uncertain too.

name: Euclid
years: about 325 BC - about 265 BC (dates are estimates)
who: A geometry teacher in Alexandria who wrote a book that was used for about 2,000 years
story: Euclid taught mathematics in Alexandria, in Egypt, about 2,300 years ago. Little is known about his life, but his book the Elements is famous. It was used to teach geometry for about 2,000 years. Euclid put many ideas in a careful order and proved each step from simple facts. In Book I he shows that two parallelograms on the same base and between the same two parallel lines have the same area, even if one looks more slanted. So cutting a shape and sliding a piece can change how it looks without changing its area. Euclid wanted a reason for every claim, just as you do when you explain your working.
link: Today you cut and rearrange shapes and explain what happens to area, which is the idea in Euclid's rule for parallelograms.
blurb: Euclid taught maths in Alexandria about 2,300 years ago. His book the Elements shows that a slanted shape with the same base and height as a rectangle has the same area.
q: A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm high. Slide its top side along to make a slanted shape with the same base and height. What is the area of each? Which has the longer way round?
a: Rectangle: 8 x 5 = 40 square cm. The slanted parallelogram has the same base and height, so its area is also 40 square cm. Its slanted sides are longer than 5 cm, so it has the longer way round (a bigger perimeter).

name: Emmy Noether
who: A German mathematician who found a link between symmetry and things that stay the same
story: Emmy Noether was born in Erlangen, Germany, in 1882. When she wanted to study mathematics at university, women were only allowed to sit in on classes if the teacher gave permission. She kept going, and in 1907 she earned her doctorate. For years she worked without pay, and for a time her lectures in Göttingen had to be advertised under another professor's name. Still she carried on. In 1918 she proved an idea now called Noether's theorem. It says that when something in nature has a kind of symmetry, a matching quantity stays the same. Symmetry is not only pretty. It tells us deep things.
link: Today you explore symmetry, and Emmy showed that symmetry is useful as well as beautiful.
blurb: Emmy Noether, born in Germany in 1882, kept studying maths even when women were not welcome at university. She showed that symmetry is useful as well as beautiful.
q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have? How many does a rectangle that is not a square have?
a: A square has 4 lines of symmetry (2 through the middles of opposite sides and 2 along the diagonals). A rectangle that is not a square has 2 (through the middles of opposite sides).

name: Florence Nightingale
who: A British nurse who used charts to show people what the numbers meant
story: Florence Nightingale was born in Florence, Italy, in 1820. She is best known as a nurse, but she also loved numbers. During the Crimean War in the 1850s she collected figures about the hospitals for soldiers. They showed that many more soldiers became sick from dirty, crowded conditions than from the fighting. She knew that long lists of numbers are hard to read, so she drew special charts to make the facts easy to see. Her ideas helped to bring in cleaner, safer hospitals. In 1858 she became the first woman elected a Fellow of the Statistical Society of London. A clear table or graph can help people make better decisions.
link: Today you read tables and line graphs, and Florence used tables and charts to make numbers easy to understand.
blurb: Florence Nightingale was a nurse who also loved numbers. She drew charts so that people could see the facts about hospitals at a glance.
q: Temperatures: 9 am 26 degrees, noon 31 degrees, 3 pm 33 degrees, 6 pm 29 degrees. Between which two times did it rise the most, and by how much?
a: 9 am to 12 noon: it rose by 5 degrees (31 - 26). Noon to 3 pm: it rose by only 2 degrees. So the biggest rise was 9 am to 12 noon, by 5 degrees. (Between 3 pm and 6 pm it fell by 4 degrees.)

name: Terence Tao
country: Australia (born in Adelaide); now also works in the USA
who: An Australian mathematician who first entered an international maths contest aged ten
story: Terence Tao grew up in Adelaide, Australia. He enjoyed maths so much that he took university maths classes while still a schoolboy. In 1986 he entered the International Mathematical Olympiad, a contest where school students from many countries solve hard puzzle-style problems. He was only ten, the youngest competitor ever, and he won a bronze medal. In 1987 he won silver, and in 1988 gold. He is still the youngest ever winner of each of the three medals. As an adult he became a professor, and in 2006 he won the Fields Medal, a top prize in mathematics. Hard problems are for practising, and trying again is part of the plan.
link: Today is Challenge Day, with competition-style puzzles like the ones in the Olympiad that Terence Tao entered three years in a row.
blurb: Terence Tao, from Adelaide, Australia, entered a maths Olympiad at age ten and won a bronze medal. He tried again each year and won silver, then gold.
q: Use guess and check: a farm has hens and cows. Together they have 10 heads and 28 legs. How many hens and how many cows?
a: 6 hens and 4 cows. Check: 6 + 4 = 10 heads; 6 x 2 + 4 x 4 = 12 + 16 = 28 legs. (Try 5 cows: 20 + 10 = 30 legs, too many; 3 cows: 12 + 14 = 26, too few.)
